title: Local belonging is stronger in psychological safety and relationships than in perceived civic influence
source_unit: American Immigration Council Center for Inclusion and Belonging, Belonging Barometer 2026; SSRS probability-based survey waves and qualitative interviews
geography: United States; national adults with age, income, partisan, race/ethnicity, education, and local-news comparisons

denominator.unit: U.S. adults across three SSRS Opinion Panel survey waves

qualitative_interviews.unit: in-depth interviews with selected survey respondents

observations.method: Three national probability-based SSRS Opinion Panel waves followed by 16 qualitative interviews; the Barometer uses ten items across belonging, psychological safety, agency/efficacy, and social connection.
observations.uncertainty: The three waves are repeated cross-sections rather than a single respondent panel; the qualitative sample is purposive and the study measures perceived belonging, not objective inclusion or civic outcomes.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults; the study reports subgroup comparisons by age, income, party identification, race/ethnicity, education, and media use.
observations.counterinterpretation: Belonging may reflect local tenure, relationships, health, mobility, safety, housing, or prior community participation; the index does not identify which intervention produced a feeling of belonging.

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the three-wave study

psychological_safety.value: over two-thirds feel comfortable expressing opinions in their local community

social_connection.value: most report satisfying relationships, while about one-third report feeling valued

local_agency.unit: approximately one in four believing they can influence outcomes or local decision-making

observations.method: Additive-index analysis of ten Barometer items covering authenticity, voice, equality, inclusion, emotional connection, relationships, insider status, and influence.
observations.uncertainty: The rounded headline shares summarize distributions across separate items and should not be read as a single composite prevalence; agreement does not establish actual voice in institutional decisions.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults in the national survey; dimensions are reported at population level with selected subgroup models.
observations.counterinterpretation: People may feel safe and connected without wanting formal influence, or may influence decisions through informal relationships not captured by the item; low agency can also reflect realistic perceptions of institutional scale.

observations.period: November–December 2025; age and income pattern in strong local belonging

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in model-adjusted survey estimates

strong_belonging_by_age.unit: model-adjusted share reporting strong local belonging

strong_belonging_by_income.unit: model-adjusted share reporting strong local belonging

predictors.value: age and income are positively associated with local belonging in regression models

observations.method: Model-adjusted predicted probabilities controlling for demographic and media characteristics; cross-sectional regression analysis.
observations.uncertainty: Associations do not establish that age or income causes belonging; life stage, housing stability, health, mobility, family, and local institutional access may mediate the pattern.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults grouped by age and household income.
observations.counterinterpretation: Older or wealthier respondents may have longer local tenure, more time, stronger networks, or greater civic access; the pattern should not be reduced to individual attitude.

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in model-adjusted survey estimates

local_news_belonging_pattern.value: strong local belonging rises with more frequent local-news consumption, reaching 47% among those consuming local news multiple times a day

national_news_belonging_pattern.value: national-news frequency was not a significant predictor of local belonging in the reported model

interpretation.value: locally relevant information may provide recognition and a sense of participation that national information does not supply

observations.method: Regression models of local belonging with media-consumption variables and demographic controls; media use and belonging are measured at the same time.
observations.uncertainty: The association may run in either direction or reflect local media markets, community interest, education, political identity, or pre-existing attachment; it is not evidence that local news causes belonging.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults by frequency of local and national media consumption.
observations.counterinterpretation: People who already feel connected may seek local news more often; local-news content and quality vary substantially across markets and platforms.

related_sources.claim: Publisher presentation documents the sample, index items, distributions, and model-adjusted relationships.
Publisher research brief associated with the 2026 Belonging Barometer study.
related_sources.access_boundary: Publisher PDF returned a 403 during retrieval; the landing page and accessible publisher presentation were used instead.

boundary: This record identifies a U.S. belonging pattern in which psychological safety and relationships are stronger than perceived local agency, with age, income, and local-news use associated with stronger belonging. It does not establish causal effects, objective political influence, equal treatment, durable participation, or that local news creates belonging.
